title: GOD COULD HAVE LED YOU AROUND THE VALLEY—SO WHY DID HE LEAD YOU THROUGH IT?
paragraphs:
GOD COULD HAVE LED YOU AROUND THE VALLEY—SO WHY DID HE LEAD YOU THROUGH IT?
Understanding Psalm 23:4 — The Terrifying Difference Between God Abandoning You in the Darkness and the Shepherd Walking You Through It
There is a sentence in Psalm 23 that most of us love to quote…
until we are forced to live it.
“Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death…”
We put it on funeral programs.
We print it on wall art.
We whisper it beside hospital beds.
We underline it when life hurts.
But there is something unsettling hidden inside Psalm 23 that we rarely stop long enough to face.
David does not say the Shepherd always keeps the sheep away from the valley.
He says he walks through it.
And maybe that is exactly where you are right now.
You prayed for God to remove the problem.
It stayed.
You prayed for the relationship to heal.
It broke anyway.
You prayed for the door to open.
It remained shut.
You prayed for clarity.
Heaven seemed silent.
You prayed for the night to end…
and somehow morning still feels very far away.
So now a question you are almost afraid to say out loud has begun forming somewhere beneath all your Christian answers:
“God… if You are really my Shepherd, why am I here?”
That question does not necessarily mean you have no faith.
David had faith.
David also knew valleys.
And Psalm 23 contains something far more powerful than the promise of a painless life.
It contains the promise of a present Shepherd.
The original Hebrew of Psalm 23:4 reads:
גַּם כִּי־אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת לֹא־אִירָא רָע כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי
Gam ki-elekh begei tsalmavet, lo-ira ra, ki-attah immadi.
“Even though I walk through the valley of deep darkness, I will fear no evil, because You are with me.”

The familiar English expression “the valley of the shadow of death” is beautiful and deeply rooted in Christian memory. But the Hebrew word צַלְמָוֶת — tsalmavet can also communicate the idea of profound or deadly darkness.
That matters.
Because this verse is not restricted to the final moments before physical death.
It speaks into places where darkness becomes so thick that you cannot see what God is doing.
Grief can become tsalmavet.
Betrayal can feel like tsalmavet.
Loneliness can feel like tsalmavet.
The consequences of your own sin can become a valley.
A season where prayers seem unanswered can feel like a valley.
Watching something you desperately wanted collapse in front of you can feel like a valley.
There are valleys where nothing has physically killed you…
but something inside you feels as though it is dying.
And David says:
“I walk.”
Do not miss that word.
אֵלֵךְ — elekh.
“I walk.”
David does not say, “I built my house there.”
He does not say, “I surrendered there.”
He does not say, “I discovered that the valley was my permanent identity.”
He says…
“I walk.”
The valley is real.
But it is not necessarily your final destination.
Somebody reading this has confused a chapter with the ending.
You thought because God allowed you into this place, this must be where your story finishes.
No.
Keep walking.
You may be crying while you walk.
Keep walking.
You may not understand while you walk.
Keep walking.
Your prayers may sound weaker than they did six months ago.
Keep walking.
You may have to limp.
Keep walking.
You may have nothing left to say except, “Jesus, help me.”
Say it…
and keep walking.
Because Psalm 23 does not describe a sheep wandering accidentally into darkness while the Shepherd frantically searches for it.
Read what comes immediately before the valley.
“He leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.”
Then:
“Yea, though I walk through the valley…”
The Shepherd has not disappeared between verses three and four.
That changes everything.
It does not mean every tragedy is something God delights in causing.
Scripture never gives us permission to call evil good.
We live in a fallen world scarred by sin, suffering, death, human rebellion, injustice, disease, and consequences.
Sometimes we suffer because other people sin.
Sometimes we suffer because we sin.
Sometimes we suffer simply because creation itself is groaning under the curse of the Fall.
And sometimes Scripture explicitly shows God leading His people into difficult places for purposes they cannot initially understand.
Israel was led toward the Red Sea before God divided it.
Jesus Himself, after His baptism, was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
So we must never flatten every valley into one simplistic explanation.
You cannot look at every suffering person and confidently announce, “God did this because He wanted to teach you something.”
Be careful.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do beside somebody who is bleeding is stop explaining their wounds and start weeping with them.
But this we can say with biblical confidence:
No valley can place the child of God beyond the presence of the Shepherd.
And sometimes God does something even more mysterious.
He does not immediately remove the valley.
He reveals Himself inside it.
David's confidence is astonishing.
He does not say:
“I will fear no evil because there is no evil.”
There is evil.
He does not say:
“I will fear no evil because I understand everything.”
He doesn't.
He does not say:
“I will fear no evil because the valley is actually pleasant.”
It isn't.
He says:
לֹא־אִירָא רָע
Lo-ira ra.
“I will fear no evil.”
Why?
Here is the center of the entire verse.
Maybe even the center of the entire Psalm.
כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי
Ki-attah immadi.
“Because You are with me.”
Not because David suddenly understood the map.
Because he knew the Shepherd.
And something beautiful happens in the grammar of the Psalm.
Before the valley, David speaks about God.
“He makes me…”
“He leads me…”
“He restores me…”
“He guides me…”
Then darkness comes.
And David stops merely talking about God.
He talks to God.
“You are with me.”
“Your rod…”
“Your staff…”
The valley turns theology into conversation.
The Shepherd who was “He” in the pasture becomes “You” in the darkness.
Maybe that is one reason some valleys change us so profoundly.
In comfortable seasons, it is possible to know information about God.
But there are nights when information alone cannot carry you.
You need Him.
There are truths about Jesus you can learn from a sermon.
There are other truths about His sufficiency that become painfully precious at 2:17 in the morning when everyone else is asleep and you are crying where nobody can see you.
There are things you learn about prayer when the answer comes quickly.
There are different things you learn when all you can pray is:
“Jesus…”
And somehow His name becomes the whole prayer.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
You smiled at church.
Nobody knew.
You answered, “I'm okay.”
You weren't.
You posted something encouraging while quietly wondering who was going to encourage you.
You prayed for everyone else while your own heart was collapsing.
You knew the right verses.
You knew the right Christian language.
You knew God was good.
But knowing it intellectually and trusting Him while walking through darkness felt like two completely different things.
And perhaps you even felt guilty about struggling.
Listen carefully.
Psalm 23 does not shame the sheep for being in a valley.
The presence of darkness is not proof of the absence of God.
And difficulty is not automatically evidence that you missed His will.
Sometimes obedience itself travels through painful terrain.
Look at Jesus.
If anyone ever perfectly followed the Father's will, it was Christ.
Yet perfect obedience did not lead Him around suffering.
It led Him toward a cross.
Gethsemane was not proof that the Father had lost control.
Calvary was not an accident.
Jesus was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
And He entered a darkness deeper than any metaphorical valley we will ever understand.
The Shepherd became the Lamb.
The One who said, “I am the good shepherd” laid down His life for the sheep.
And here the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Our deepest problem was never merely that life hurts.
Our deepest problem was sin.
We were not simply wounded sheep needing encouragement.
We were sinners needing reconciliation with a holy God.
We had wandered.
“All we like sheep have gone astray.”
And Jesus did not stand at a safe distance shouting directions back home.
He came for us.
The Good Shepherd laid down His life for His sheep.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
Then on the third day…
the tomb lost.
Death did not get the final sentence.
Jesus rose.
That means Psalm 23 is not merely motivational poetry telling hurting people to think positively.
For the Christian, the Shepherd has scars.
Jesus has walked into death itself and emerged victorious.
So when Christ says He will never abandon His people, our hope is not wishful thinking.
Our Shepherd has already confronted the ultimate enemy.
And won.
That is why the Christian can walk through valleys without pretending they do not hurt.
Christian courage is not denial.
Faith does not mean you never cry.
Faith does not mean you never tremble.
Faith does not mean you never ask questions.
Faith means that somewhere beneath the tears, beneath the confusion, beneath the trembling, your soul keeps returning to one stubborn truth:
“You are with me.”
David continues:
“Thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.”
The rod and staff were not decorative accessories.
They represented the shepherd's active care.
Guidance.
Protection.
Authority.
Rescue.
The sheep could not protect itself from every danger.
It needed a shepherd.
So do we.
And perhaps that is one of the humiliating mercies of the valley.
It exposes the illusion that we were ever self-sufficient.
Green pastures can sometimes make us forget how desperately we need the Shepherd.
Valleys remind us.
When money cannot fix it…
when connections cannot fix it…
when intelligence cannot fix it…
when your image cannot fix it…
when another motivational quote cannot fix it…
when you finally reach the end of yourself…
you discover that Jesus was never supposed to be an accessory to your strength.
He is your Savior.
Maybe the valley is exposing something in you right now.
Maybe God is showing you that you loved control more than you realized.
Maybe the thing you called “peace” was actually just favorable circumstances.
Maybe the thing you called “faith” had never yet been tested.
Maybe you have spent years looking Christian while privately keeping certain rooms of your life locked from Christ.
Maybe your valley was partly created by choices you knew were wrong.
If so, grace does not mean pretending sin does not matter.
Grace calls you home.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling the wandering sheep away from destruction.
Jesus did not die so we could become comfortable with the very sin that nailed Him to the cross.
He died to forgive us, reconcile us to God, and transform us.
So if the darkness has exposed something hidden…
bring it into the light.
Stop performing.
Stop bargaining.
Stop blaming everyone else.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop trying to manage what Christ is calling you to surrender.
Repent.
Not because Jesus hates you.
Because the Shepherd is calling you back.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding even from the people closest to you, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
Let that comment become more than engagement.
Let it become a prayer.
And then talk to God when nobody is watching.
Confess what He already knows.
Receive the mercy purchased by Christ.
Because there is something else Psalm 23 refuses to let us forget.
The valley is verse four.
It is not verse six.
There is more story after the darkness.
There is a table.
There is an overflowing cup.
There is goodness.
There is covenant love.
There is the house of the Lord.
David eventually says:
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.”
The Hebrew word translated “follow” is astonishingly strong.
יִרְדְּפוּנִי — yirdefuni.
It comes from a verb often carrying the idea of pursuing or chasing.
Think about that.
David had enemies pursuing him.
But he understood that there was another pursuit greater than theirs.
God's goodness and covenant love were after him.
You may feel hunted by your past.
Grace is pursuing you.
You may feel chased by regret.
Mercy has not stopped following.
You may think your worst chapter permanently disqualified you.
Look at the cross.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven, rebels reconciled, captives liberated, the guilty justified, the broken restored, and wandering sheep brought home through Jesus Christ.
That is our story.
Not because our scandal did not matter.
Not because sin suddenly became harmless.
But because Jesus paid what sinners could never pay and offers what sinners could never earn.
Maybe your valley will not end tomorrow.
I will not insult your pain by promising that it will.
The Bible does not promise every Christian immediate earthly deliverance from every hardship.
Some prayers are answered differently than we expected.
Some losses leave scars.
Some questions may remain unanswered this side of eternity.
Some faithful believers die still waiting for things they prayed to see.
But Scripture gives us something greater than the promise that every valley will disappear on our preferred schedule.
It gives us Christ.
And ultimately it gives us resurrection.
The final destination of God's redeemed people is not the valley.
Revelation gives us a future where death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally be no more.
Until then…
we walk.
Sometimes through pasture.
Sometimes beside quiet waters.
Sometimes through darkness.
Sometimes before enemies.
But never outside the reach of the Shepherd.
Maybe you have been asking:
“Why didn't God take me around this?”
I cannot tell you the hidden reason behind every valley.
Anyone claiming to know God's secret purpose behind every tragedy claims more than Scripture allows.
But perhaps Psalm 23 invites us to ask another question:
“Who is walking with me through it?”
That changes the valley.
Not because darkness suddenly becomes light.
But because you discover you were never walking alone.
The Shepherd is here.
When you cannot feel Him.
He is here.
When prayer feels dry.
He is here.
When your future looks uncertain.
He is here.
When everybody else seems to be celebrating while you are surviving.
He is here.
When you have to repent of how badly you handled this season.
He is here.
When you have done everything you know to do and all you can whisper is His name.
Jesus.
He is here.
And perhaps one day you will look backward and realize something extraordinary.
You thought the greatest miracle would have been God preventing the valley.
But one of the miracles was that the valley did not get to keep you.
You walked through.
Not because you were unbelievably strong.
Because the Shepherd was faithful.
So if you are reading this from your own valley, do not disappear into isolation.
You do not have to explain everything.
And if God has already brought you through a valley you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what Christ has done. Your testimony may become the rope another exhausted believer grabs tonight.
You may never know whose midnight prayer God answers through something you were willing to share.
Because valleys have a strange way of making us forget in the darkness what we knew in the light.
Come back when you need the reminder:
כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי — ki-attah immadi — “because You are with me.”
Salvation cannot be purchased, and financial support is never a condition for glorifying God.
We glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience, love, generosity, worship, service, and lives surrendered to Him.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of stewardship when done freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully.
Leave surrendered.
Open your Bible.
Return to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
Pray again.
Walk again.
Trust again.
And bring somebody with you.
And comment if this reached somewhere deeper than you expected.
“I'm still walking. Jesus is with me.”
Let somebody else scrolling through the comments see that they are not the only believer fighting to keep trusting God.
Because perhaps the sentence your valley needs most tonight is not:
“God will explain everything.”
It is simpler.
Older.
Stronger.
כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי
Ki-attah immadi.
Because You are with me.
The valley may become part of your testimony…
but because of Jesus, it does not get to become your identity.
The Shepherd has not abandoned the story just because you have reached the darkest page.
